**What the law says**

- **Advertising:** A provider or agent "must not advertise or otherwise offer premises to let" unless, when advertising, they "reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards." The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard:** Schedule 4, clause 8 says "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty before occupation:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough?**

The documents don't say what evidence is needed to prove a breach. Two points matter, though:

- A photo may show visible mould, but the standard only covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A photo alone may not show the cause, so it may not establish a breach on its own.

Visible mould in the ad photos may be relevant to that belief, but the documents don't say how much weight it carries.

The governing law is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111**, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026, which covers 1 February 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Landlord's right:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession." If the landlord has a contract of sale with conditions, the notice must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If there is an unconditional contract, it must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into. The termination date must be **at least 90 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be in writing and signed by **both** the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements:** A notice given under this section is of no effect if its termination date is earlier than the end of the fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Possession:** A landlord can only get a possession order from the Tribunal (VCAT) if the notice has not been withdrawn. The Tribunal must also be satisfied the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that it is reasonable and proportionate to make the order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Enforcement:** Rental providers cannot personally use force to remove a renter. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT order (warrant for possession) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Check the notice.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason, and be accompanied by the documentary evidence the Director approves. Its termination date must be at least 90 days after it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge its validity at VCAT.** You can apply within **30 days after the notice to vacate is given**, on or before the hearing of any possession application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Note that the no-lease-break-fee protection in section 91ZB(5) does not apply to renters who end the agreement on receipt of such a notice, so check your agreement for any fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get advice.** Form 6 directs renters who may have grounds to challenge a notice to seek advice immediately from community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or call 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Section 68 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), sets this duty [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** If the agreement doesn't contain a prescribed safety term, the landlord must ensure an electrical safety check of the installations, appliances and fittings they provide is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Describe the tripping and when it happens, and keep a copy.
2. **A repair by a suitably qualified person.** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Section 91ZZR says nothing in the challenge subdivision affects any right to challenge the validity of another notice to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal considers the landlord's conduct:** When deciding whether a possession order is reasonable and proportionate, the Tribunal must consider "the behaviour of the residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Check whether it cites a ground that actually applies to you (for example, a rent, damage or danger ground). A reason that doesn't match a listed ground, or that lacks specifics, may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [1, s 91ZZQ]. Nothing in the documents says that a sale falling through withdraws the notice automatically.
- **Sale-based notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 90 days after the notice is given [1, s 91ZZB(1), (4)]. A notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, state the reasons, include the approved documentary evidence supporting the reason, and state the termination date [1, s 91ZZO].
- **Possession orders:** The landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order after the notice. VCAT must be satisfied the notice "has not been withdrawn" [1, s 330(1)(a)(ii)], and that it is "reasonable and proportionate" to make the order [1, s 330(1)(f)]. VCAT cannot decide the application before the termination date in the notice [1, s 329].
- **Enforcement:** Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only on a VCAT order (a warrant for possession). Rental providers cannot personally use force to remove you [2, Schedule 1 Form, cl 4].
- **Re-letting:** After possession from a sale notice, the landlord must not let the premises for use as a residence within 6 months of the notice, unless VCAT decides otherwise [1, s 91ZZH].

1. **Check the notice.** Confirm that the termination date is at least 90 days after it was given, that it is in the prescribed form, and that documentary evidence was attached [1, ss 91ZZB(4), 91ZZO].
2. **Ask the landlord in writing** whether they will sign a notice of withdrawal. Under the Act, that needs both signatures [1, s 91ZZQ].
3. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You may apply to challenge the validity of a sale-based notice "on or before the hearing of an application for a possession order," and the application must be made "within 30 days after the notice to vacate is given" [1, ss 91ZZS(1)–(2)]. The 30-day window matters, so act quickly.
4. **Seek advice.** The Regulations' form suggests contacting a community legal organisation, or Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or 1300 558 181 [2, Schedule 1 Form, cl 6].
5. **If you decide to leave,** you can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice, and you are not liable for a lease break fee in that case [1, s 91ZB(2), (5)]. Note that the 14-day reduced period under s 91ZB applies where the notice to sell was given under s 86 and you were not told of the proposed sale before signing the agreement [1, s 91ZB(1)(e)].

**Short answer:** The documents don't set a minimum number of circuits. They do require that power outlets and lighting circuits be protected by compliant breakers and safety switches, and that the landlord keep the home in good repair. You can ask the landlord to fix the problem.

## What the law says

- **Circuits:** The rental minimum standard says that, from 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and to a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't specify how many circuits a rental must have, or whether overloading that trips a breaker breaches this standard.
- **Landlord's duty:** The landlord must ensure the rental complies with the minimum standards on or before the day you move in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for an individual or 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must also keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition, whether or not you knew of the disrepair when you moved in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for or do

1. **Urgent repairs:** If the premises don't meet the minimum standards, you may give the landlord a request for urgent repairs to bring them into compliance [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Give this in writing. The Form 1 standard terms say the landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Reimbursement:** If you arrange urgent repairs yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them and they haven't, the landlord may reimburse the reasonable cost up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Electrical safety check:** The landlord must have an electrical safety check every 2 years, and must give you the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A copy of the most recent check must be given to you within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Qualified repairers:** Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Record the problem:** Note the issue on your condition report and keep photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). **What the law says (as at 1 February 2026)**

Two documents were in force on that date: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111, dated 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 005, dated 25 November 2025, in force until 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

- The provider "must give a renter at least 90 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice "may only provide for one rent increase" and must state the amount, how it was calculated, and your right to apply for a review [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- For a fixed-term agreement, rent cannot be increased during the term unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for a formal notice.** Request a Form 5 notice stating the current rent, the new rent, the start date, and the calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The notice must be in writing. Also check whether your agreement is fixed-term, and when the rent last increased, since a second increase within 12 months would breach the rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the start date.** A valid notice must give at least 90 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the notice gives a shorter period, the documents indicate it does not comply.
3. **Apply for a review if you receive a valid notice.** You may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria "within 30 days after the notice is given" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT within 30 days after the Director's report, or within 30 days of the notice if there is no report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the payment rule.** Form 5 states that you "will need to pay the increased rent amount from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This applies only if you receive a valid notice, so you should not assume you must pay the higher amount from the date in the email.

**Limits of the documents**

- The documents do not say whether an email from an agent could ever count as a valid notice, or how VCAT would treat one. They say only that a non-compliant increase is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not say what happens if you have already paid the higher amount. If you have, get advice on recovering it.
- Regulations 21A and 21B, which change how the Director and VCAT assess excessive rent, take effect on 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so they do not apply on 1 February 2026.

If you receive a valid notice, or want to dispute the email, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

Retaliation for repair requests is not expressly listed for the repair-related notices (s 91ZX) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your agreement is month to month, so the fixed-term rules don't apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Form and content:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, states the reason(s), states the termination date, and, for certain grounds, comes with documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice period:** For the repair ground (s 91ZX), the termination date must be at least 90 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 2. **The prescribed form.** Is it the Form 6 notice to vacate? Check that it is signed, addressed to you, and dated. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
3. **The termination date.** Check it against the minimum period for the section cited. A notice given the same day as your repair request with a very short date is worth examining. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. **Documentary evidence.** For repair-related or several other grounds, the notice must be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Your repair paper trail.** Confirm you gave written notice of the leaking fixtures as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note the dates of your request and the notice. This evidence matters for showing timing.

- **Challenge at VCAT.** Form 6 says you may challenge a notice if you believe it was given because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter, or if it was not given properly or the reason is wrong [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). - **Repair requests.** If the repairs are not done within 14 days of your written notice, you can apply to the Director (s 74) or VCAT (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same about non-urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Advertised rent must be fixed.** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [1, s 30F(1)].
- **No inviting higher offers.** A provider or agent must not solicit or invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [1, s 30F(3)].
- **No accepting higher offers.** A provider or agent must not accept an unsolicited or uninvited offer of rent higher than the advertised amount [1, s 30F(4)].
- **Penalties.** The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 penalty units for a body corporate [1, s 30F].
- **Misleading conduct.** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, or through a false or misleading representation about the rent payable [1, s 30E(2)–(3)]. The Act notes that Tribunal orders may be made for contraventions of this section [1, s 30E note].
- **Discrimination.** If the withdrawal or rejection was based on a protected attribute, the Act prohibits discrimination in refusing to let premises [1, s 30A]. A person who has suffered loss from unlawful discrimination may apply to VCAT for compensation under s 210AA [2, Form 3, item 8].

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** to explain the withdrawal email and to confirm the basis for it. Applicants are told to contact the rental provider or agent to check the outcome of an application [2, Form 3A, Part B, Information for the applicant, item 2]. 2. **Ask whether the advertised rent was a fixed amount** and whether the agent solicited or accepted a higher offer. If so, the conduct appears to fall within s 30F(3) or (4) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
